doc.title: Language Features
doc.paragraph:
In this section, you will be guided through the features of Adaptive Script. If you know ECMAScript (JavaScript),
lists where the two are the same and where they differ.

Variables in Adaptive Script are used to identify a memory location, and are declared using the let or const keywords. A variable is visible from its declaration to the end of the block it is declared in.
Adaptive Script does not have classes. Values have Adaptive data types, and what you can do with them is provided by functions.

At this time, Adaptive Script does not support importing code from other locations. The only way to share code between scripts is to store them in qualified variables that would be accessible to scripts.

Adaptive Script can annotate values with Adaptive data types (integer, string, arrays, object shapes, unions, and more). Annotations are always accepted; optional type checking (off by default) can catch mismatches at compile time and/or runtime. See the Types section for syntax and flags.

Adaptive Script supports closures. A nested function can access variables from an enclosing scope and keep those bindings after the outer scope has finished, so later calls still see the values that were in force when the function was created.
Nested function declarations and function values returned from other functions both capture enclosing let / const bindings (and parameters).
Every statement ends with a semicolon.
An expression on its own is not a statement: a call, an assignment, ++, and -- are.
Adaptive Script provides try/throw/catch/finally exception handling.

In Adaptive Script, throw is a statement that requires a string (the error message). Write optional data and then any value to store on the error object. Write optional id and then a string that sets the error object's id (for example not_found) so an uncaught error can use that name's HTTP status. After the message, data is only the clause name, so a variable also named data is throw "…" data data.

The catch statement always receives one error object, which contains the message and data that was thrown. The catch binding may be a simple name or a list/object Pattern (same destructuring as let / const), for example catch ({ message, data }). The object also has an id (mnemonic such as throw, not_found, or denied) and a numeric errorCode. Branch on id. If the error is not caught, an HTTP request uses that code's mapped status (for example not_found is 404). general is the default code when nothing more specific applies.

Function and lambda parameters may be a simple name or the same list/object Pattern used in let / const (holes, defaults, rest, rename, nesting, string keys, and computed keys). Parameter defaults may be any Expression. At a call site, f(...array) expands an array into separate arguments (in addition to definition-side ...rest formals). See the Language Reference Function statement for examples.

A script function may be declared : void. A void function is a procedure, like a built-in declared void (print()). The call is the void singleton, not undefined and not the body’s last assignment, so f(); as a statement does not change the script result. An untyped script function that never completes still yields undefined as the call result, which does set the script result.

Object and array behavior is provided by Adaptive functions in the environment, not by methods on shared type objects. Optional method-style calls such as obj->keys() or arr->push(1) are available when a function is a data-type method (the receiver is the first parameter).

Helpers include property listing (keys, values, entries), indexing (at), stack and queue mutators (push, pop, shift, unshift, splice), creating a fixed-length array of undefined entries (create_array), immutability (freeze), and quantifiers (every / some, same family as all_of / any_of). Array literals may omit a value between commas (that entry is undefined). See the Language Reference section Objects and Arrays and the Function Reference categories object, array, and higher_order_array.

Object property names in an object value may be an identifier, a string literal, or an expression in square brackets. Bracket expressions are evaluated when the object value is evaluated; the result is used as the property name (a string). This is the same idea as obj[expression] for get and assignment. Variable and parameter names remain lexical identifiers.

At this time, Adaptive Script does not support generators or user-defined iterators. Arrays can be iterated with for-of. Objects are iterated by walking keys, values, or entries (for example for (let pair of entries(o))).
At this time, Adaptive Script does not support asynchronous operations.
The evaluate function runs a string as code.
Code inside an evaluate call may not access or change any variables outside of its scope.
The switch statement can use a function to compare the value with each case (using).
A script may include a #compile pragma to control whether type checking runs for that script. The Types section lists the environment flags and the matching #compile options.

#compile strictDouble; (flag compile:strictDouble) makes IEEE 754's invalid operation and division by zero exceptions errors for that script, the way a C compiler option can reject what the language allows. Without it, doubles follow IEEE 754's default handling: 0.0 / 0.0 is NaN and 1.0 / 0.0 is Infinity. With it, those are errors, as are Infinity - Infinity, sqrt(-1.0) and log(0.0), and <, <=, >, >= are IEEE 754's signaling comparisons, an error for a NaN. What IEEE 754 does not call one of those exceptions is unchanged: overflow gives an infinity, a NaN operand passes through arithmetic, and == is the quiet compare. The pragma applies to the script it is in, wherever its functions are called from.

A compiler literal is a # name for a value the compiler already knows. It is a value in an expression, not a statement and not a function call. These are not the same as the #compile pragma or the #block forms used when decompiling.

list.item: #pi, #e, #ln2, #ln10, #log2e, #log10e, #sqrt2, #sqrt1_2: π, e, ln 2, ln 10, log2 e, log10 e, √2, and √½, for the math functions (cos(#pi), log(#e)).
#doubleMax, #doubleMin, #doubleMinSubnormal, #doubleEpsilon: IEEE double limits. #doubleMin is the smallest normal double (C's DBL_MIN) and #doubleMinSubnormal the smallest subnormal one.

#integerMax, #integerMin: the 64-bit integer limits. #integerMaxExactDouble, #integerMinExactDouble: the range (9,007,199,254,740,991 either way, 2^53 - 1) where every integer converts to a double and back unchanged, and survives a JavaScript client reading the JSON.
#infinity (alias #inf), #minusInfinity, #nan: the same as Infinity, -Infinity and NaN. The # forms are preferred, and decompile writes them; the reserved words keep working.
